steps: Map your current site to the new one page by page, using your analytics and search data, and mark each page to keep, merge or retire.

Build conditional content rules so one email shows a different block to each persona or segment, agreeing the wording of each block with your team.
Test each conditional block with test leads from every persona or segment, and record which actions use send-time optimization and why.
deliverables: Send-time optimization on agreed email actions
Conditional content rules by persona or segment
asks: Content for each persona or segment's block, approved by your team
A marketing lead who agrees where send timing matters
MO11.risk: The wrong block shown to a persona or segment: we test every block with test leads from each group before the email goes live.
MO11.outcome: Selected journey emails go out at the time each profile is predicted most likely to engage, and one email shows each persona or segment its own block.
phrases: one email with different blocks per segment

steps: Map your marketers by role, from email authors to journey builders, and plan the sessions each group needs.
Train every group on the Home page, where they start AI conversations, launch skills and open marketing workspaces, and on programs and people lists.
Train journey builders and email authors on the marketing workspace, journeys and email authoring, with exercises built on your own programs.

deliverables: Handover walkthrough with your team lead
asks: The names and roles of the marketers to train
Your naming rules, or a lead who can agree them
MO12.risk: Marketers publishing journeys or emails without the agreed checks: we train on your own programs and hand over a publishing checklist each team follows.
MO12.outcome: Your marketers work in Marketo Optimizer on their own, from the Home page to published journeys and emails, following your naming rules.

steps: Review journey results, email performance, list membership and traffic control decisions each month, using the Coworker chat interface to explore journey metrics.
Agree the changes with your marketing lead, then tune audiences, path prompts and score weights, recording each change and its reason.
Report the month's findings and next steps to your team, comparing results before and after each change made the previous month.
deliverables: Monthly journey and audience review report
Tuned audiences, path prompts and score weights
asks: A marketing lead who agrees the changes each month
Notice of new campaigns, products or audiences that affect journeys
MO13.risk: Too many changes at once hide what worked: we agree a short list of changes each month and compare results against the month before.
MO13.outcome: Each month your journeys, audiences, path prompts and score weights are reviewed and tuned, with findings and next steps reported to your team.

steps: Create the Marketo Qualifier and Marketo Qualifier Admins user groups in your Admin Console, with the names and product profile Adobe specifies.

Opt-out footer on every outbound email

Approved opt-out footer wording from your legal team

MQ01.outcome: Your representatives, administrators and managers reach Marketo Qualifier through the right user groups, and every outbound email carries your opt-out footer.
phrases: email performance report access for managers

steps: Work with your CRM administrator to set up the connected app or app registration, with the read-only access the first connection needs.
Enter the Salesforce or Microsoft Dynamics 365 connection in Marketo Qualifier, and agree whether to grant the write access that activity synchronization and opt-out write-back need.

Marketo Qualifier connected to your CRM

Build a first activity report in CJA with your team to check the dimensions, and record the setup in a short runbook.
Check each activity before launch: that its activity type is supported, and that its reporting source is CJA with the agreed data view, since the source cannot change once live.
deliverables: Target datasets in your CJA connection
Activity and experience dimensions with persistence and labels
asks: A data team contact who manages your CJA connection and data views
The data view your teams agree to use for Target reporting
TC01.risk: An activity launched with the wrong reporting source, which cannot change once live: we check every activity against a pre-launch checklist.
TC01.outcome: Your Target activities report in Customer Journey Analytics, with activity and experience dimensions ready for activity reports on the agreed data view.
phrases: set up Target reporting in CJA
CJA data view for Target activities

steps: Agree the success metrics for Target activities with your optimization team, and how each one is defined in CJA.
Build Experimentation panel reports for your live Target activities, showing lift and confidence on the agreed success metrics.
Build a reusable Workspace template from those reports, so each new Target activity is read with the same layout and success metrics.
Walk your optimization team through reading lift and confidence in the reports, using one of your own activities.
deliverables: Experimentation panel reports for your Target activities
asks: Your optimization team's success metrics, with an owner for each
A list of the Target activities to report on first
TC02.risk: Calling a winner before the result is clear: the reports show confidence beside lift, and we train your team to read both before deciding.
TC02.outcome: Your team has Experimentation panel reports and a reusable Workspace template for Target activities that report in Customer Journey Analytics, with lift and confidence on your agreed success metrics.
phrases: report test winners on business KPIs

steps: List your current Analytics for Target (A4T) activities by type with your optimization team, and agree which activity types move to CJA reporting.
Set the reporting source to CJA per activity or account wide, as agreed, and keep a record of which activities report where.
Give your Target users the Experience Platform role they need, and check that each one can open the new reports.
Show your team how activity reports in CJA compare with what they used in Adobe Analytics through A4T.
deliverables: Reporting source set per activity or account wide
Experience Platform roles for Target users
asks: Your optimization team's list of current activities and who relies on their reports
An administrator who can assign Experience Platform roles to your Target users
TC03.risk: Teams losing sight of results during the move: we agree which activity types move and when, and record where each activity reports.
TC03.outcome: The agreed Target activity types report in Customer Journey Analytics, your Target users have the access they need, and everyone knows where each activity reports.
phrases: move test reporting off Adobe Analytics
Adobe Analytics to CJA migration for testing
switch reporting source for Target activities
Target users access to CJA reports

steps: Agree with your personalization team the journey audiences to build in CJA and the personalization activities each one will serve.
Build the journey audiences in CJA, check their sizes with your team, and publish them to Experience Platform.
Share them with Target through the Adobe Target destination, in Real-Time CDP or Journey Optimizer, using a Target-enabled datastream.
Check that each audience appears in Target for the agreed personalization activities, and record each audience's definition and activities.
deliverables: Audiences shared through the Adobe Target destination
Record of each audience and its activities
asks: The journeys and behaviors your personalization team wants to act on
Access to your Target-enabled datastream and the Adobe Target destination
TC04.risk: Personalizing on audiences nobody can explain later: we record each audience's definition and the activities that use it, so your team can trace every experience.
TC04.outcome: Audiences built on journeys in Customer Journey Analytics reach Target for your agreed personalization activities, each one traced to its definition.
phrases: journey analytics audiences in Target activities

steps: Agree the pages, activity types and data Target needs with your web and analytics teams, and record them in an implementation plan.
Enable Target in the datastream and add flicker handling, testing it on your key pages so default content does not flash before an experience appears.
Render Visual and Form-based Experience Composer activities, and pass the profile and entity data your activities and audiences will use.
Validate the setup with test activities on each page type, checking that experiences render and data arrives, and record the results in a validation log.
deliverables: Target enabled in the datastream, with flicker handling
Profile and entity data passed to Target
Validation log with test activity results
asks: A web developer who can deploy changes to your site's pages
The pages and data your first activities will need, agreed with your marketing team
TG01.risk: Visitors seeing default content flash before an experience appears: we add flicker handling and test it on your key pages before any activity goes live.
TG01.outcome: Target is enabled on your pages, ready for A/B tests and Experience Targeting activities built in the Visual or Form-based Experience Composer.
phrases: pass profile and entity data to Target
migrate Target from at.js to Web SDK
validate Target tagging on key pages

steps: Agree with your Target administrator who does what in Target, then add your users and assign their roles from the agreed access list.
Create workspaces, user groups and properties where you have Target Premium, and add the at_property parameter to your Target implementation.
Set up the reporting, environment and starting audience settings, and test them with a sample activity before your first live test.
Record users, roles, workspaces, properties and settings in an administration record your team keeps current.
deliverables: Workspaces, user groups and properties, where used
Reporting, environment and starting audience settings
asks: The people who will use Target, and what each one will do
A Target administrator to approve roles and workspace access
TG02.risk: Teams changing each other's activities: we agree roles, workspaces and properties before the first activity is built, and test access with each role.
TG02.outcome: Your team works in Target with the right roles, workspaces and settings in place, ready to build its first activities.
phrases: separate Target workspaces by brand or region
control who can approve and launch tests

steps: Run an ideation and prioritization workshop with your marketing, product and analytics leads, and rank ideas by business alignment, level of effort and potential impact.
Write an activity plan for each top idea, with its hypothesis, audience, success metrics and the decision a result will drive.
Build the first A/B and Experience Targeting activities, and QA each one across pages, devices and audiences before launch.
Launch the first activities once each passes QA and its plan is signed off, and hand each plan and QA record to the team that will read its results.
deliverables: Activity plans with hypotheses and success metrics
First live A/B and Experience Targeting activities
asks: Marketing, product and analytics leads for the ideation and prioritization workshop
Sign-off on each activity plan and its success metrics before build
TG03.risk: Tests that end without a clear answer: every activity plan sets its hypothesis and success metrics before build, so each result drives a decision.
TG03.outcome: You have a ranked testing roadmap and your first A/B and Experience Targeting activities live, each with a plan that defines success.
phrases: prioritize tests by effort and impact
launch first A/B tests in Target
QA and launch first Target activities

steps: Agree whether you recommend products or content, on which key pages, and the catalog attributes the recommendations will draw on.
Set up the product or content catalog feed, and check a sample of items against your source catalog after the first load.
Pass item, category and cart data on the key pages with your web developers, and test that each page sends the expected values.
Set the global exclusions and Recommendations settings, review the first recommendations with your merchandising or content team, then launch them.
deliverables: Item, category and cart data on key pages
asks: A catalog owner who can supply the product or content feed and answer attribute questions
A web developer to add item, category and cart data to key pages
The items or categories that must never be recommended
TG04.risk: Items you never want shown appearing in recommendations: we set the global exclusions first and review the first recommendations with your team before launch.
TG04.outcome: Your key pages show recommendations drawn from your product or content catalog, within the global exclusions you set.

steps: Pick the next activities from the roadmap each month with your team, and write each one's plan with its hypothesis and success metrics.
Design, build and QA the month's activities, then launch each one with an agreed audience and run time.
Analyze the results of finished activities by audience, reading lift and confidence on the success metrics each plan chose.
Share readouts and next steps with stakeholders, and add new ideas to the roadmap through one repeatable intake.
deliverables: Launched A/B and Experience Targeting activities
asks: A standing monthly review with the stakeholders who act on test results
New test ideas from your teams, sent through the agreed intake
TG05.risk: A program that stalls between tests: we keep a ranked roadmap and one repeatable intake, so the next activities are ready when the last ones end.
TG05.outcome: New activities go live from your roadmap each month, and your stakeholders get readouts by audience with clear next steps.
phrases: build and QA new Target activities monthly

steps: Run discovery workshops with each team to map how work is requested, planned, reviewed and delivered today, and record each process in a process map.
Agree the structure of groups, teams and job roles with your leads, and set them up in Workfront with the system preferences.
Stand up a governance board with named roles for the rollout, and agree how it decides on changes, standards and priorities.
Turn the process maps into a rollout plan that names which processes move into Workfront first and what each later step builds.
deliverables: Groups, teams, job roles and system preferences in Workfront
Governance board charter with named roles
asks: A lead from each team for the discovery workshops
Named people for the governance board, with time set aside for its meetings
Your organization chart, or a list of teams and job roles
WF01.risk: Setup that copies today's workarounds into Workfront: we map each process first and agree changes with the governance board before building.
WF01.outcome: You have mapped processes, a Workfront structure of groups, teams and job roles, and a governance board ready to steer the rollout.
phrases: configure groups, teams and job roles

steps: Agree what each audience needs to see and do, for requesters, project managers, creatives and approvers, in an access and layout plan.
Assign access levels by license type, which set the limits within which people share objects with view, contribute or manage permissions.
Build a layout template for each audience, so requesters, project managers, creatives and approvers each see the parts of Workfront they use.
Assign the templates to groups, teams and job roles with your Workfront system administrator, who makes the team and job-role assignments, then test each one.
deliverables: Access and layout plan by audience
Access levels assigned by license type
asks: Your Workfront system administrator, to make the team and job-role assignments
The list of users with their license type and audience
WF02.risk: People seeing too much or missing what they need: we test each layout template and access level as a sample user of that audience.
WF02.outcome: Each person opens Workfront with access suited to their license type and a layout built for their role, from requester to approver.
phrases: Workfront access levels by license type
Workfront views for requesters and approvers

steps: List every kind of request your teams take, who submits it, who receives it and what it must include, in an intake inventory.
Set up each request queue as a project in the Queue Details area, with queue topics for the request types it takes.
Build a custom form for each request type, and add routing rules that send each request to the right user, job role, team or project.
Test sample requests of every type from submission to the receiving team, and fix forms or routing before the queues open.
deliverables: Request queues with queue topics and routing rules
Custom forms for each request type
asks: The kinds of requests each team takes today, with examples of complete requests
A lead from each receiving team to approve its form fields and routing
WF03.risk: Requests that arrive incomplete or land with the wrong team: we test sample requests of every type end to end before the queues open.
WF03.outcome: Every request is submitted the same way, arrives with what the work needs, and goes to the right team.
phrases: custom forms for each request type
standardize how work requests are submitted

steps: Pick the repeatable work to template, such as campaigns, content and launches, and walk through recent real projects with the people who ran them.
Draft each project template with its tasks, durations, roles and custom forms, and agree it with the team that runs that work.
Add the approvals each template needs, using reusable approval templates with multi-stage approvals or parallel paths where the review calls for them.
Pilot each template on a live project, adjust tasks and durations from what the pilot shows, and hand over the final version.
deliverables: Project templates for the agreed repeatable work
Pilot results and template change notes
asks: Examples of recent campaign, content and launch projects, with the people who ran them
A template owner in each team to sign off its template
WF04.risk: Templates built from how work should run rather than how it does: we draft from recent real projects and pilot each template before rollout.
WF04.outcome: Your teams start repeatable work from project templates with the tasks, durations, roles, approvals and forms already in place.
phrases: multi stage review and approval setup
task durations and roles in templates

steps: Plan training by role for administrators, project managers and requesters, with exercises built on your own processes and projects.
Start with one basic process, such as a simple request, and train each role on it until it runs end to end in Workfront.
Add further processes in stages once the first one runs, with short sessions for each role at every stage.
Set up regular training sessions for new and existing users, with materials your administrators can run themselves.
deliverables: Training sessions and materials for each role
Regular training schedule for new and existing users
asks: The names and roles of the administrators, project managers and requesters to train
One basic process to start with, and the team that runs it
WF05.risk: Too much change at once: we start with one basic process and add the rest in stages, so people learn on work they know.
WF05.outcome: Your administrators, project managers and requesters each use Workfront for their part of the work, and new users are trained on a regular schedule.
phrases: train project managers and requesters in Workfront
ongoing training for new Workfront users

steps: Run the monthly administration: add and remove users, and update forms, templates and reports as your teams' work changes.
Collect user feedback on a set cadence, through short surveys and conversations with each team, and log each request.
Bring the proposed changes to the governance board each month, then make the approved ones and report back to users.
deliverables: Change proposals for the governance board
asks: A standing slot on the governance board's agenda each month
Notice of people joining, moving or leaving, from your team leads
WF06.risk: Small requests piling up until people work around Workfront: we collect feedback on a set cadence and bring changes to the board each month.
WF06.outcome: Workfront keeps up with how your teams work, with users, forms, templates and reports updated through a steady, board-approved cycle.
phrases: maintain Workfront forms, templates and reports

steps: Agree with your Workfront administrator who will view and who will create in Workfront Planning, and record each user's license and permissions in an access list.
Assign the Workfront and Planning licenses and the Workfront Planning permissions to each user, and add the license types to their access levels.
Assign a layout template that shows Planning to Contributor and Light users, then test each license type with a sample user before rollout.
deliverables: Access list of users, licenses and permissions
Access levels updated with the license types
Layout template showing Planning to Contributor and Light users
asks: The list of people who will view or create in Workfront Planning
A Workfront administrator to approve the access level and layout template changes
WP01.risk: Users who cannot find Planning or can change more than they should: we test each license type with a sample user before rollout.
WP01.outcome: Each of your users opens Workfront Planning with the right license and permissions, and Contributor and Light users find Planning in their layout.
phrases: Planning layout template for Light users
who can view or create planning records

steps: Run planning workshops with each team to map its work lifecycle and the things it plans, such as campaigns, products, regions and personas.
Design the workspaces, the record types, their fields and how they connect, including connections to Workfront projects, in a model your team signs off.
Build the workspaces from a predefined template or from scratch, with your own record types, fields and the connections between them.
Test the model with real examples from each team, adjust fields and connections, then share each workspace with the agreed users, groups and teams.
deliverables: Workspaces, record types and fields built
Connections between record types and to Workfront projects
asks: A lead from each team that plans work, for the workshops and sign-off
Your current planning spreadsheets or documents, to show how each team plans today
Decisions on which record types each workspace holds and who owns them
WP02.risk: A model that fits one team and not the next: we test it with real examples from every team and adjust it before rollout.
WP02.outcome: Your teams plan in Workfront Planning workspaces that match how they work, with campaigns, products and other record types connected to one another.
phrases: record types for campaigns and products
planning record types, fields and connections
connect planning records to Workfront projects
planning workspace built from a template

steps: Collect your planning spreadsheets, agree which ones move, and map each sheet and column to a record type and field in a mapping sheet.
Clean the data with its owners: remove duplicates, align names and values, and fill or flag the gaps before anything is imported.
Import each record type from a CSV or Excel file with its records and fields, starting with a pilot sheet your team checks.
Check the connections between the imported records against the source sheets on a sample, and fix any that did not link.
deliverables: Imported record types, fields and records
asks: Your current planning spreadsheets, with an owner for each one
Decisions on duplicate or conflicting records, from the people who own the data
WP03.risk: Duplicates and mismatched names breaking connections: we clean and align the data before import and test a pilot sheet first.
WP03.outcome: Your existing plans are in Workfront Planning as records with their fields and connections, so teams start from current data, not empty workspaces.
phrases: import planning spreadsheets into Workfront Planning
map spreadsheet columns to record fields

steps: Agree with your teams and leaders which views each audience needs, such as a marketing calendar or a campaign timeline, and the fields each one shows.
Build the table, timeline and calendar views, with the filters, groupings and fields each audience needs.
Review each view with its audience on real records, and adjust the filters and groupings before handing it over.
Share each view with its audience, since views are shared separately from the workspace, and check that each person sees the intended records.
deliverables: Shared table, timeline and calendar views
asks: The teams and leaders who will use each view, and what they need to see
Time from each audience to review its views on real records
WP04.risk: Views that show too much or too little: we build each one for an agreed audience and review it with that audience on real records.
WP04.outcome: Your teams and leaders each open a shared view, such as a marketing calendar or campaign timeline, showing the records and fields they need.
phrases: calendar and timeline views of plans
filtered table views of planning records
planning views grouped by region or channel
see upcoming launches on one calendar

steps: Agree which record types you take requests for, the fields each request form asks for, and who approves which requests.
Create a request form for each agreed record type, and add approval rules by field value so each request reaches the right approver.
Test sample requests through every approval rule, then share each form with the people who submit to it.
Hand over a short guide to submitting and approving requests, with the list of forms, rules and approvers.
deliverables: Request forms for the agreed record types
Test results and a short request guide
asks: The record types you take requests for, and who submits each one
The approvers for each kind of request, and the field values that route to them
WP05.risk: Requests that reach the wrong approver or none: we test sample requests through every approval rule before the forms are shared.
WP05.outcome: Requests arrive as complete records through one form per record type, and each goes to its approver by the rules you agreed.
phrases: request form for new campaign records
approval rules based on field values
intake form that creates planning records

steps: Agree the questions each leader needs answered from Planning records, and whether each report belongs in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard or your own reporting tool.
Build the agreed reports on your Planning records in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard, laid out around the questions each audience asked.
Prepare the Planning data in Workfront Data Connect where reports belong in your own tool, and agree the fields your reporting team receives.
Check each report's figures against the records in Workfront Planning, and walk each audience through its reports.
deliverables: Reports in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard
Planning data in Workfront Data Connect, where used
asks: The questions your leaders want answered from planning data
A contact for your own reporting tool, if reports will be built there
WP06.risk: Reports that disagree with the records: we check each report's figures against Workfront Planning before handing it over.
WP06.outcome: Your leaders follow planning in reports built on your Planning records, in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard or in your own reporting tool.
phrases: Workfront Data Connect for planning data
planning data in Power BI or Tableau
planning data in Snowflake for reporting

steps: Plan the rollout team by team, with an order, a start date and a named lead for each team, in a rollout plan.
Teach each team the Planning terms first, since Workfront Planning has its own concepts and terminology, even for people who know Workfront.
Train each team to add, connect and view records in its own workspace, with exercises on its own plans.
Hand over a short guide for workspace owners, and walk each owner through it before their team starts.
asks: A lead from each team to set its dates and gather its people
Time from each team for training in its own workspace
WP07.risk: People who know Workfront assuming Planning works the same way: we teach the Planning terms first and practice in each team's own workspace.
WP07.outcome: Each team adds, connects and views its own records in Workfront Planning, and workspace owners have a guide for everyday upkeep.

end user training for Workfront Planning

steps: Gather change requests from workspace owners each month, and add the record types, fields and views your planning now needs.
Tidy records and connections with their owners, removing duplicates and stale records and fixing connections that no longer link.
Adjust sharing for people who join, move or leave, and send a monthly note of the changes made.
deliverables: Monthly changes to record types, fields and views
asks: A workspace owner in each team to send change requests each month
Notice of people joining, moving or leaving the teams that use Planning
WP08.risk: A model that drifts as teams add fields on their own: we make every change from one request list and record it in the monthly note.
WP08.outcome: Your Workfront Planning model keeps pace with how you plan, with clean records, working connections and sharing that matches your teams.
phrases: monthly Planning record type and field changes
add views as planning needs change
adjust workspace sharing as teams change

steps: Agree the first event-triggered messages, such as cart, browse or welcome, and the scheduled sends, with the event, audience and profile attributes each one reads.
Set up each event-triggered message in Journey Optimizer to listen for its behavioral or system event and deliver a contextual message to the triggering profile.
Build the scheduled sends as campaigns on the agreed Real-Time CDP audiences, keeping sensitive attributes out unless you approve them.
Test entry, conditions and suppression for each message against an agreed set of test cases, including people who should not receive it, and record the results.
deliverables: Event-triggered messages for the agreed events
Scheduled sends on agreed Real-Time CDP audiences
Test cases and results for entry, conditions and suppression
asks: Your first messages, with the events, audiences and attributes each may use
Approved content for each message and the person who signs it off
XA01.risk: A message reaching the wrong people: we test entry, conditions and suppression with agreed test cases before any message reaches customers.
XA01.outcome: Your first event-triggered messages and scheduled sends run in Journey Optimizer on Real-Time CDP audiences and profile attributes, tested before they reach customers.

behavioral triggered messages from profile data

steps: Map each journey with your marketing team in a design sheet: its entry audience or event, branches, waits, conditions, exit criteria, and channel and content.
Build the journeys in Journey Optimizer, entering from the agreed Real-Time CDP audiences or events, with the waits, conditions and message actions from the design.
Set the exit criteria and the configured conditions that route each profile to the agreed channel and content.
Walk test cases through every branch, wait and exit before each journey goes live, and record the path each one took for your sign-off.
deliverables: Journeys built on Real-Time CDP audiences or events
asks: A marketing lead who owns each journey and approves its design
Approved content for every message in each journey
XA02.risk: A profile stuck in a branch or sent too many messages: we test every path, wait and exit with test cases before each journey goes live.
XA02.outcome: Your branching, multi-touch journeys run in Journey Optimizer from Real-Time CDP audiences or events, routing each profile to the agreed channel and content.
phrases: lifecycle journeys such as onboarding and renewal
journey entry, exit criteria and conditions
journeys that start from audience membership
route customers to channels by behavior

steps: Build the offer catalog in Journey Optimizer Decisioning from an offer sheet agreed with your marketing team, naming the owner and intended audience of each offer.
Set the eligibility rules on Real-Time CDP audiences and attributes, keeping sensitive attributes out unless you approve them.
Configure the ranking strategies and placements, adding behavioral recommendation strategies where your catalog is large, so each profile gets the next-best offer or content.
Test the decisions with test cases for each audience, confirm that no profile receives an offer it is not eligible for, and review the rankings with your team.
deliverables: Offer catalog in Journey Optimizer Decisioning
Eligibility rules, ranking strategies and placements
Behavioral recommendation strategies, where the catalog is large
asks: Your offers and content, with an owner who approves each one
Your business rules for who may see each offer
Your rules on which attributes may be used to choose offers
XA03.risk: An offer shown to someone it was not meant for: we test eligibility rules with test cases for each audience before any placement goes live.
XA03.outcome: Your customers get the next-best offer or content from centralized decision logic in Journey Optimizer Decisioning, on the agreed placements across your channels.

steps: Agree the web and app surfaces to personalize, and what each one shows identified and anonymous visitors, in a personalization plan with your team.
Check that signed-in visits send a person-level identifier, such as a CRM ID or a hashed email, so Experience Platform stitches each visit into the profile.
Configure profile-based personalization for identified visitors on the agreed surfaces, delivering content, offers or promotions by real-time profile and segment membership.
Set up anonymous web personalization on captured behavioral signals and edge audiences, then test both paths with consent given and refused before launch.
deliverables: Personalization plan for the agreed surfaces
Anonymous web personalization on edge audiences
Test results, with consent given and refused
asks: The web and app surfaces you want personalized, and who owns each
Approved content, offers and promotions for each audience

XA04.risk: Personalization that ignores a visitor's consent choice: we test every surface with consent given and refused before it goes live.
XA04.outcome: Identified visitors see content, offers or promotions based on their real-time profile, and anonymous visitors see content based on their behavior on your site.
phrases: personalize content for logged in users
in app personalized content and offers

personalized banners and promotions on site
personalization for anonymous and authenticated visitors

steps: Agree with your personalization team the audiences and profile attributes to share with Target for the first activities, keeping sensitive attributes out unless you approve them.
Configure the Adobe Target destination and its workspace in Real-Time CDP, using the datastream for your site.
Share the agreed audiences and profile attributes to the Adobe Target connection, and check that they appear in Target.
Walk your Target users through the shared audiences and attributes, ready for the first activities, such as A/B tests or Experience Targeting.
deliverables: Adobe Target destination and workspace configured
Agreed audiences and profile attributes shared to Target
Check record for the first activities
asks: Your personalization team's list of audiences and attributes for the first activities

XA05.risk: Sharing attributes that should stay private: we agree the attribute list with your team and share only those, checking each one in Target.
XA05.outcome: Your Real-Time CDP audiences and profile attributes are available in Target, ready for the first web and app personalization activities.

steps: Agree with your team the audiences that should qualify in real time, and the pages where same-page or next-page personalization applies.
Set up the datastream with the Target and Experience Platform services and edge segmentation, so the agreed audiences qualify in real time.
Run test visits to check that each agreed audience qualifies in real time and that its experience shows on the same page or the next.
Record the results and the datastream settings in a short runbook for your team.
deliverables: Datastream with Target, Experience Platform services and edge segmentation

asks: The audiences and pages your team wants personalized in real time

XA06.risk: An audience that qualifies too late for the visit it was meant for: we test each one with test visits before your team relies on it.
XA06.outcome: Visitors qualify for the agreed audiences in real time, so Target can personalize the page they are on or the next one they open.

Agree with your marketing team which offer decisions from Journey Optimizer Decision Management to test, and the lift and conversion goals that count.
Place the offer decisions in manual A/B Test or Experience Targeting activities in Target, and set up the agreed lift and conversion goals.

deliverables: Target activities serving Journey Optimizer offer decisions
Lift and conversion goals in each activity

XA07.outcome: Your manual A/B Test and Experience Targeting activities in Target serve offer decisions from Journey Optimizer, measured on the lift and conversion goals you agreed.

steps: Document with your data team the permitted collection and dataset route for the agreed concierge interaction data, without reusing the Brand Concierge-bundled datastream or dataset for other uses.
Test which clicks, form submissions, booked meetings and live chats arrive through that route, and record what each one carries.

steps: Map with your privacy and legal team the laws you must meet, such as GDPR, CCPA or rules for your sector, and which data uses need consent or an opt-out.
Connect your consent management platform to every Adobe script on your pages, such as the Web SDK through setConsent, with each region's default consent set before a visitor chooses.
Apply data usage labels to personal and sensitive fields where data is activated or messages are sent, and set consent policies, which need Healthcare Shield or Privacy and Security Shield.
Set up access and delete requests through Privacy Service for the products it covers, with a runbook and request log for each system that handles requests on its own.
Test before launch with consented, refused and withdrawn profiles on each page and channel, confirm opted-out people stay out of audiences and sends, and run sample access and delete requests.
deliverables: Privacy requirements map signed off by your team
Consent integration design for your site and channels
Data labels and policy configuration record
Privacy request runbook and consent test results
asks: A privacy or legal lead who confirms the laws that apply and signs off the consent design
Your consent management platform, its consent categories, and an admin who can change its settings
topics.risk: Consent collected but not acted on downstream: we test every channel and activation with refused and withdrawn profiles before launch, and hand over the tests for later changes.
topics.outcome: Your customers' consent and privacy choices are designed into how you collect, store and activate data and tested before launch, while you stay responsible for your own legal compliance.

facts.text: The Web SDK's setConsent command tells it whether to send data (opt in), discard data (opt out) or use the default consent setting (consent unknown).
facts.quote: The setConsent command tells the Web SDK if it should send data (opt in), discard data (opt out), or use defaultConsent (consent unknown).
facts.title: Experience League: setConsent (Web SDK)

facts.text: When an audience is first activated, Policy Service checks the data usage labels in the audience, the destination's marketing purpose and which profiles consented under your consent policies.
facts.quote: When an audience is first activated, Policy Service checks for applicable policies based on the following factors: The data usage labels applied to fields and datasets within the audience to be activated. The marketing purpose of the destination. The profiles that have consented to be included in the audience activation, based on your configured consent policies.
facts.title: Experience League: Automatic policy enforcement

facts.text: Consent policies need your organization to have purchased the Adobe Healthcare Shield or Privacy and Security Shield add-on.
facts.quote: Consent policies are currently only available for organizations that have purchased the Adobe Healthcare Shield or Privacy and Security Shield add-on offerings.
facts.title: Experience League: Work with consent policies in Journey Optimizer

facts.text: Adobe Experience Platform Privacy Service is built to support privacy requests for several Adobe applications.
facts.quote: Adobe Experience Platform Privacy Service is built to support privacy requests for several Adobe CX Enterprise applications.
facts.title: Experience League: Privacy Service and CX Enterprise applications

facts.text: Operational Telemetry on your Adobe Experience Manager site uses no client-side state or ID, such as cookies or localStorage, to collect its usage metrics.
facts.quote: AEM Operational Telemetry does not use any client-side state or ID, such as cookies or localStorage, sessionStorage or similar, to collect usage metrics.
facts.title: aem.live: Operational Telemetry

topics.title: Your own CDN in front of the site
steps: Map your CDN setup with your CDN team: who owns it, the change windows, our access, the paths each origin serves, and which changes we prepare and your team applies.
Build a stage configuration on your CDN that points each path to its origin, such as the Edge Delivery origin, whose cache headers set the TTL, or the AEM-managed CDN.
Set up purging: push invalidation in the production CDN configuration on Edge Delivery, or for the AEM-managed CDN its purge API token and a matching purge on yours.
Review security with your security team: enforce HTTPS, set the X-AEM-Edge-Key where your CDN sits in front of the AEM-managed CDN, and keep the edge rules your policy requires.
Run load, caching, purge, redirect and page speed tests on stage, then switch your CDN's origin, or DNS where the hostname changes, and hand your CDN team a runbook.
deliverables: Load, caching, purge and page speed test results
Security settings record signed off by your team
asks: A CDN engineer on your team with console access, on call through cutover and after launch
Your CDN change windows and the security rules your policy requires
topics.risk: Changes held up by CDN access or change windows: we agree owners and windows in discovery and prepare each change for your CDN team to apply.
topics.outcome: Your CDN stays in front of the site, with caching, purges, HTTPS and security rules tested on stage before your live traffic switches over.

facts.text: By default, Adobe Commerce on Cloud uses Fastly and Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service uses an Adobe-managed CDN; where you need to, you can configure your own CDN for the storefront.
facts.quote: By default, Adobe Commerce on Cloud projects use Fastly, while Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service projects use an Adobe-managed CDN service. If necessary, you can configure your own CDN, also known as “Bring Your Own CDN” (BYO CDN).
facts.title: Experience League: Commerce Storefront CDN configuration

facts.text: Push invalidation is supported on Fastly, Akamai, Cloudflare and CloudFront CDNs as well as the Adobe-managed CDN, and is enabled in your project's production CDN configuration.
facts.quote: Push invalidation is currently supported for CDNs of the following vendors: Fastly Akamai Cloudflare CloudFront Adobe Managed Push invalidation is enabled by setting the project's production CDN configuration
facts.title: aem.live: Configuring push invalidation for BYO production CDN

facts.text: On your own production CDN, the cache TTL is controlled by the origin's cache control response headers, and Adobe's setup guide says to enable origin cache control where the CDN offers it.
facts.quote: Cache TTL on the production CDN is controlled via origin cache control response headers. This should be enabled (if available).
facts.title: aem.live: BYO CDN Setup

facts.text: With AEM as a Cloud Service, your existing CDN can point to the AEM-managed CDN, provided your team manages it, has CDN engineers on call and passes a load test before production.
facts.quote: If a customer must use its existing CDN (or any kind of reverse proxy, for example a loadbalancer or a WAF), they can manage it and point it to the AEM-managed CDN, providing the following are satisfied: The customer must have an existing CDN that would be onerous to replace. The customer must manage it. The customer must be able to configure the CDN to work with AEM as a Cloud Service - see the configuration instructions presented below. The customer must have engineering CDN experts that are on call in case-related issues arise. The customer must perform and successfully pass a load test before going to production.
facts.title: Experience League: CDN in AEM as a Cloud Service

facts.text: Your team can set, in a self-service way, the X-AEM-Edge-Key header value the Adobe CDN uses to validate requests from your own CDN, and the API token used to purge the CDN cache.
facts.quote: customers can configure, in a self-service way, the following: The X-AEM-Edge-Key HTTP header value used by the Adobe CDN to validate requests coming from a Customer-managed CDN. The API token used to purge resources in the CDN cache.
facts.title: Experience League: Configuring CDN Credentials and Authentication

topics.title: Page speed and Core Web Vitals
steps: Measure your current site's Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse scores for each key template, on mobile and desktop, as the baseline we compare against after launch.
Agree a Lighthouse score per key template for release tests, and Google's good thresholds for real visitors: LCP 2.5 seconds, INP 200 milliseconds and CLS 0.1, at the 75th percentile.
Build each template so what the first screen needs loads first and third-party tags load last, and check that the CDN caches pages, code and images.
Test every release against the agreed Lighthouse score before it goes live, and hold any change that drops a key template below its target until it is fixed.
Track real visitors' Core Web Vitals after launch against the agreed thresholds and the baseline, find the pages and elements that slow them down, and fix the worst first.
deliverables: Baseline and target scores for each key template
Third-party tag inventory with a load plan
A performance test in every release
asks: Access to your current site's analytics and any Core Web Vitals reports, for the baseline
The owners of your third-party tags, to agree which tags stay and when each one loads
topics.risk: Third-party tags added after launch slowing pages again: we agree with your tag owners that each new tag passes the same release test, and watch real visitor data.
topics.outcome: Your key templates launch at their agreed Lighthouse scores, every later release is tested against them, and real visitor data shows any page that slips.

facts.text: On Edge Delivery Services, each pull request runs PageSpeed Insights against its test pages, and the AEM GitHub bot fails it if the score is below 100, with a small buffer for variation.
facts.quote: When you open a pull request (PR) on a project, the test URLs in the description of your project are used to run the PageSpeed Insights Service against. The AEM GitHub bot will automatically fail your PR if the score is below 100 with a little bit of buffer to account for some volatility of the results.
facts.title: aem.live: Web Performance, Keeping your Lighthouse Score 100

facts.text: In Adobe's Keeping it 100 guidance, the delayed phase of page loading holds third-party tags and other assets that are not material to the experience.
facts.quote: Phase D (Delayed): This contains everything else such as third-party tags or assets that are not material to experience.
facts.title: aem.live: Web Performance, Keeping your Lighthouse Score 100

facts.text: Adobe's launch checklist for the Adobe Commerce storefront has you record Web Vitals and Lighthouse baselines, so site speed can be compared before and after launch.
facts.quote: Separately, record Web Vitals and Lighthouse baselines using Performance best practices so you can compare site speed before and after launch.
facts.title: Experience League: Commerce Storefront launch checklist

facts.text: On AEM Sites, Experience Audit gives the median Google Lighthouse scores for the pages you configure and the difference from the previous scan.
facts.quote: Experience Audit provides the median Google Lighthouse scores for the configured pages and the difference in score to the previous scan.
facts.title: Experience League: Experience Audit dashboard

facts.text: Every AEM site, including AEM Sites as a Cloud Service sites without Edge Delivery Services, collects sampled metrics by default, and Operational Telemetry gives you an interface to explore that data for your domain.
facts.quote: Every AEM Site, including Adobe Experience Manager Sites as a Cloud Service without Edge Delivery Services, collects metrics and data by default. This data is sampled, and used by Adobe to diagnose issues around performance, traffic acquisition, and conversion for customer sites. With Operational Telemetry, Adobe offers a simple user interface to explore the collected data for a given domain.
facts.title: aem.live: Operational Telemetry explorer

topics.title: A/B testing without Adobe Target
steps: Agree a test plan with your team for each test: the hypothesis, one primary metric such as form starts, guardrail metrics, the sample size and the run time.
Build the challenger as a copy of the control page that changes one thing, such as the headline or call to action, and keep it out of search indexes.
Send the experiment ID and the variant each visitor sees into your analytics data with every page view and conversion, so each result can be split by variant.
Check each variant before launch: preview both pages, confirm the tracking records the right variant, start with an even traffic split, and check the split again once real traffic arrives.
Decide each test at its planned sample size from the primary metric's lift and confidence by variant, then publish the winner as the page and log the learning.
deliverables: Test plan with hypothesis, metrics and sample size
Challenger pages, kept out of search indexes
Experiment and variant tracking in your analytics
Results readout and learnings log for each test
asks: The page to test, the change you want to try and the metric that decides it
An owner on your team who approves each test plan and signs off each result
topics.risk: Calling a winner too early on too little traffic: we set the sample size and run time before launch, and decide only when the test reaches them.
topics.outcome: Each A/B test on your pages runs to an agreed plan, with each visitor's variant in your analytics, and you keep only the changes the results support.

facts.text: On Edge Delivery Services, an experiment uses the page you already have as the control, and a challenger page you create replaces it for some of your visitors.
facts.quote: Experiment variants are the easiest way to get started with experimentation. This approach uses the page you already have as the control, you then create a challenger page that will replace the control for some of your visitors.
facts.title: aem.live: Experimentation

facts.text: In AEM as a Cloud Service, the experimentation rail is the main way to set up experiments, on a project in an Edge Delivery Services context or in the Universal Editor.
facts.quote: The experimentation rail is your primary way to set up experiments. It can be used with your project either in an Edge Delivery Services context or in the Universal Editor.
facts.title: Experience League: Contextual Experimentation in AEM as a Cloud Service

facts.text: In Customer Journey Analytics, the Experimentation panel compares variations to find which best drives an outcome, and shows the lift and confidence of an A/B experiment from any experimentation platform, including your own data.
facts.quote: The Experimentation panel lets analysts compare different user experiences, marketing, or messaging variations to determine which is best at driving a specific outcome. You can evaluate the lift and confidence of any A/B experiment from any experimentation platform: online, offline, from Adobe solutions like Target or Journey Optimizer, and even BYO (bring-your-own) data.
facts.title: Experience League: Experimentation panel in Customer Journey Analytics

facts.text: For the Experimentation panel, two dimensions in your data view, one for the experiment and one for the variant, carry the Experimentation Experiment and Experimentation Variant labels; without these labels the panel does not work.
facts.quote: In your data view that contains experimentation data, pick two dimensions, one with the experimentation data and one with the variant data. Then label those dimensions with the Experimentation Experiment and the Experimentation Variant labels. Without these labels present, the Experiment panel does not work, since there are no experiments to work with.
facts.title: Experience League: Experimentation panel in Customer Journey Analytics

facts.text: In Adobe Analytics, once an eVar is set for a visitor, Adobe keeps that value until it expires, and success events the visitor reaches while it is active count toward it.
facts.quote: When an eVar is set to a value for a visitor, Adobe automatically remembers that value until it expires. Any success events that a visitor encounters while the eVar value is active are counted toward the eVar value.
facts.title: Experience League: Conversion Variables (eVar) in Adobe Analytics
